title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to assess whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration versus plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, an artifact‑grounded sensitivity bound tied to observed discordant counts, and concrete recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration is central to NetOps. Large language models (LLMs) promise productivity gains for intent→configuration translation, but probabilistic generation can produce misordering, omission, or unsafe commands. A common mitigation pattern pairs LLM generators with deterministic validators/simulators and bounded repair loops to create a floor‑safety net. Despite many proposals and demos, preregistered controlled evaluations that quantify how tightly bounded guarded pipelines change first‑pass misconfiguration rates are scarce. We therefore preregistered and ran a narrowly scoped paired experiment whose core research question is: Can a minimal guarded pipeline (single shared LLM candidate per task + frozen deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair attempt) reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under controlled paired sampling semantics? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic seed generation and archived per‑task artifacts; (2) confirmatory statistics computed from those artifacts; (3) an explicit artifact‑grounded sensitivity bound explaining inferential limits arising from observed discordance; and (4) concrete, artifact‑anchored recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory designs.
sections.related_work: Recent system demonstrations and surveys show promise for LLMs in intent→configuration tasks but report failure modes (misordering, omission, overconfidence) relevant to safety [10.1002/nem.2313]. Work in adjacent domains demonstrates that verifier‑assisted, retrieval‑augmented, and repair‑loop pipelines reduce factual errors and improve grounding, motivating guarded NetOps architectures [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Deterministic network verification methods (e.g., header‑space analysis, specification checking) provide algorithmic foundations for validators that can statically check reachability and policy constraints without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Standards and guidance documents emphasize verifier‑assisted architectures and auditability as essential for high‑risk domains [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our experiment situates itself at the intersection of these strands by providing a preregistered, artifact‑grounded measurement of first‑pass validity under an explicit guarded pipeline.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: The study was preregistered (cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) before observing outcomes. Confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration specified a planning assumption baseline_pass_rate = 0.40 used to set sample size and expected discordant counts.

Design and sampling: Paired within‑task design with a deterministic seed list of 300 tasks. For each seed a single shared candidate from the declared generator served as the baseline response and as the starting point for guarded validation/repair (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. This shared‑candidate pairing was preregistered to reflect an operational workflow (repair of a single plan) but increases within‑pair correlation and typically reduces informative discordant pairs versus independent‑draws designs.

Model and provider constraints: The declared generation model in the execution contract and archived model configuration is gpt-5-mini. Execution accounting and model configuration are archived; in particular the authoritative recorded model configuration artifact is execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). That archived artifact records "declared_model_version": "gpt-5-mini" and "temperature": null. Explicitly: the model_configuration.json artifact records an unset/null temperature value; a null/unset temperature in that authoritative artifact is not evidence that sampling was forced deterministic (temperature=0). Therefore sampling determinism was unspecified in the recorded configuration, and nondeterministic sampling remains a possible source of generator variance; we state this here because it affects interpretation of generator‑variance related inferences and should inform follow‑up study designs.

Validator and repair: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalized each generated configuration into a normalized AST and applied static checks derived from task payloads (required_sequence, workflow policies such as must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, minimum_active_in_groups). The scoring rule 'full_intent_constraint_validation' marked success only when the validator's normalized_configuration satisfied required_sequence and expected_final_state constraints and produced no violations. The preregistered repair adapter was invoked only when validator violations appeared; it received the shared candidate and structured violation codes and was restricted to a single repair attempt aiming for minimal edits sufficient to remove violations. Post‑repair validation used the same deterministic validator.

Contamination, missingness, and analysis: The preregistration specified deterministic contamination checks (AST equality, near‑duplicate thresholds) and deterministic replacement rules from a reserve set. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) with paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Missingness handling used the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rule (drop pairs only if both calls failed). All seeds, per‑task artifacts, and analysis code were archived in the execution manifest and analysis bundle.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑derived): planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300. Model calls used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair invocation). No provider or infrastructure failures occurred. Primary outcomes (archived counts): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.6667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency (guarded vs baseline): n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Confirmatory inference (preregistered): exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Observed absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Repair (H2): the single permitted automated repair corrected the lone invalid baseline output, yielding repair success 1/1 with Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0].

Artifact‑grounded sensitivity bound: The observed discordant total is n10 + n01 = 1, which imposes a hard limit on resolvable absolute paired difference equal to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. The preregistered target (≥50% relative reduction from assumed baseline 0.40) corresponds to an absolute improvement ≈0.30 (≈90 net discordant pairs favoring guarded outputs) and therefore could not be detected given the observed near‑ceiling baseline. These numerical facts are reproduced directly from archived paired contingency and condition_summary artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation tied to artifacts. The archived contingency (n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0) fully constrains inferential outcomes: the paired difference equals (n10 − n01)/N and with only one discordant pair exact paired tests have essentially no power to detect large preregistered effects. The paired bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.01] and exact McNemar p = 1.00 both reflect this limitation.

Why the preregistered planning assumption mattered. We preregistered baseline_pass_rate = 0.40 for power planning, which implied many expected discordant pairs under the targeted relative reduction. The observed baseline (299/300) collapses that expectation. Practically, future studies must align task difficulty (or adversarial augmentation) with the desired conditional sample size of initial failures and with pairing semantics to ensure sufficient discordant pairs for the planned estimand.

Pairing semantics tradeoffs. The shared_initial_candidate design reflects an operational claim (repair of a single proposed plan) but reduces expected discordance and therefore reduces statistical signal for McNemar tests relative to independent‑draws designs. Study designers should choose pairing semantics that map directly to operational goals and incorporate that choice into power/sample‑size calculations.

Repair as a conditional estimand. H2 concerns P(repair succeeds | initial failure). Observing 1/1 repair success yields point estimate 1.0 but a wide CI [0.025, 1.0]; precise estimation of repair effectiveness requires powering for the expected number of initial failures, not merely overall N.

Construct validity and runtime semantics. Our validator applied deterministic static checks and canonicalization; it did not execute configurations in emulators or devices. Thus the results are conditional on static semantics: runtime dynamics (control‑plane convergence, transient reachability) were not measured. When runtime guarantees are required, integrating emulation/simulation stages and preregistering their mapping to success/failure is necessary.

Practical recommendations (artifact‑anchored). Based on archived artifacts, we recommend: (1) calibrate task difficulty or add adversarial seeds to ensure a nontrivial number of initial failures or target discordant counts aligned with planned absolute effects; (2) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly and reflect their impact in power calculations; (3) include emulation when runtime semantics are central to operational claims. Each recommendation is traceable to execution manifest fields (task difficulty knobs, validator violation codes, paired contingency table).
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (300 pairs) comparing single‑shot LLM generation (declared gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline consisting of a frozen deterministic validator and a single automated repair iteration. Baseline yielded 299/300 valid outputs and guarded yielded 300/300 valid outputs; the single permitted repair corrected the lone invalid baseline output. The observed near‑ceiling baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline = 0.40), eliminating statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations that aim to measure remediation or repair effectiveness should align task difficulty (or adversarial augmentation), pairing semantics, and repair budgets with the intended estimands and power calculations, and should integrate emulation when runtime guarantees are required. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (declared gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed baseline_pass_rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Shared_initial_candidate pairing increased within‑pair correlation and reduced the number of discordant pairs informative for McNemar inference.
Validation used deterministic static checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; runtime consequences were not executed and remain unmeasured.

Repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
